verses.1:
> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm

### **MEANING**

The opening gives the surah its first sound before it gives the reader a sentence: ***“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”***. These are the names of Arabic letters, recited separately rather than joined into a word. The verse does not itself explain them. Its position invites attention, but it also requires restraint: a reader should not turn a possible interpretation into a certainty the wording has not supplied. What follows immediately is a declaration about the Book, so the opening leads into revelation without being reduced to a gloss for it.

### **EARLY EXPLANATIONS**

The archive preserves several explanations from early authorities. Qatādah, through Maʿmar, and Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, call the letters a name of the Qur’an. Mujāhid is also reported through Ibn Jurayj as calling them *“openings by which God begins the Qur’an”*; that description fits the fact that the same kind of separate letters begins other surahs, including Qur’an 29:1, 31:1, and 32:1. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd, in a report carried by Ibn Wahb, treats such letter-groups as names of surahs. A report through al-Suddī attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās the explanation that the letters refer to God’s Greatest Name. A transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah and a separate report from ʿIkrimah describe them as an oath by God. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, in a report transmitted by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, gives a letter-by-letter expansion connecting them with divine names, attributes, and appointed terms. These are distinct proposals, not one agreed definition.

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Abū al-Ḍuḥā and ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib expands the letters as *“I am God, the All-Knowing.”* Mujāhid, in a report through Khuṣayf, instead calls the openings alphabetic spelling. The contrast matters: the early material does not establish one universally accepted decoding. Nor does the existence of competing explanations make the recited letters empty sounds. Their form is deliberately preserved, and the Qur’an repeatedly places such openings where they can be heard as the beginning of a new recitation.

### **THE OPENING AND THE BOOK**

The first verse also marks a transition. The following words, ***“This is the Book”***, identify what the listener has just heard as the beginning of a larger revealed address. The archive records an explanation of the letters as *“openers”* of the surahs, and also a proposed rhetorical purpose: their unusual sound could make people who had turned away pause long enough to hear what followed. That is a proposed function, not a report that every listener reacted in the same way.

The letters’ Arabic names are spoken aloud, but they are not joined into an ordinary phrase whose grammar settles their meaning. This distinction helps prevent two opposite mistakes: pretending the verse says nothing, or asserting a detailed hidden message as if the verse spelled it out. Their recurrence elsewhere gives a meaningful Qur’anic parallel, while their exact force remains contested in the transmitted explanations.

The safest reading, then, keeps both features in view: this is a purposeful opening and a genuine interpretive question. The surah moves from the sound of separate letters to the claim that revelation is a guide. The reader can acknowledge the explanations preserved by early authorities, notice the opening’s place in the Qur’an, and continue without claiming certainty where the verse itself has not furnished it.

Taken together, the range of explanations makes restraint part of the reading: one can hear a deliberate opening and acknowledge early proposals without turning any into a definitive decoding. The letters remain at the threshold of the Book; the reader can attend to what follows without pretending that the source has settled what it leaves contested.
verses.2:
> This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺

### **MEANING**

After the separate letters, the surah points to revelation itself: ***“This is the Book”***, described as free from doubt and as guidance for people who are mindful of God. The demonstrative translated *“this”* is emphatic, not a sign that the Book is distant or absent. Early explanations understand the Arabic *dhālika*, literally *“that,”* as referring to the Book now being recited, much as a speaker can point to what has just been mentioned. The opening therefore moves directly from recitation to the Book’s reliability and purpose.

### **NO DOUBT, GUIDANCE**

Early explanations gloss ***“no doubt”*** as no uncertainty about the Book. Mujāhid through Ibn Jurayj and Qatādah through Maʿmar state that meaning directly; reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās do so through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Jurayj, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas is transmitted through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar and his father. A line by the pre-Islamic poet Sāʿidah ibn Juʾayyah al-Hudhalī likewise uses ***“no doubt”*** to mean *“no uncertainty.”* The phrase is not a claim that every hearer will feel no questions. It asserts the truth of revelation, while the following verses distinguish between those who receive it and those who reject it.

The word translated as ***“a guide”*** means direction or leading along a way. Al-Shaʿbī, through Sufyān, describes it as *“guidance away from error”*; a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and other Companions through al-Suddī calls it *“light for the mindful.”* ***“For those mindful of Allah”*** identifies the people who benefit from that guidance, not a limit on whom the Qur’an addresses. The same revelation can guide the willing and stand as evidence against those who knowingly refuse it. That distinction is reflected in the next verses, which describe the traits of believers and then the responses of deniers and hypocrites.

### **WHO ARE THE MINDFUL?**

The archive preserves a range of descriptions of *al-muttaqīn*, the mindful: people who avoid what God has forbidden, carry out what is required, and place hope in God’s mercy. In a report from al-Ḥasan, transmitted through Sufyān, they avoid prohibitions and fulfill obligations. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq connects their caution with fearing the consequence of abandoning known guidance and trusting what has been brought to them. Qatādah, transmitted through Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, points forward to the qualities named in the next verse: faith in the unseen, prayer, and giving.

These are not competing definitions so much as different angles on a life oriented toward God: inward awareness expressed through action. The app’s wording, ***“those mindful ˹of Allah˺”***, preserves that practical sense without reducing mindfulness to anxiety. The verse’s sequence is important: the Book is guidance, and mindfulness is the disposition that allows a person to follow it. Qur’an 6:92 similarly describes revelation as a blessed Book, making its guidance a gift that calls for a responsive life.

The archive also preserves less common referents: some take the demonstrative to point to revelations sent earlier, or to the Torah and Gospel. Such readings make grammatical sense as references to something already known, but the repeated early gloss that it means the Book being recited gives the immediate line its clearest force. This distinction is helpful: the word *“that”* can point across a discourse, while the app’s *“this”* makes the present recitation vivid. Neither rendering changes the central claim that the Book is a source of guidance.
verses.3:
> who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them

### **MEANING**

This verse makes the mindful person’s response concrete. They trust realities beyond immediate sight, maintain prayer, and give from what God has provided. The three descriptions join inward conviction, regular worship, and material responsibility. The wording does not present belief as a private opinion separated from conduct: what a person trusts shapes how they worship and how they use their resources. Nor does the verse name one narrow form of giving; its broad expression keeps the emphasis on generosity as a response to provision.

### **FAITH IN WHAT IS UNSEEN**

Early explanations understand ***“the unseen”*** broadly. A report through al-Suddī, carrying explanations attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and other Companions, includes Paradise, the Fire, and what God has described in revelation. Qatādah, transmitted by Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, names the Garden, the Fire, resurrection, and the Day of Judgement. A report from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, transmitted by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, also includes God, angels, messengers, the final meeting, and life after death. The common point is trust in realities not available to ordinary sight, including the revelation that tells people about them.

The archive records a disagreement about the people described across verses 2:3–4. A report through al-Suddī, carrying explanations attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and other Companions, distinguishes the believers among the Arabs here from People of Scripture in the next verse. Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, treats the opening verses together as a description of believers. That difference concerns how the passage groups its audience, not whether the listed qualities matter. Prayer and giving are presented alongside faith, not as optional additions to it.

### **PRAYER AND GIVING**

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq, Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad, and either ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explains ***“establish prayer”*** as performing its obligations. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, carried by Abū Rūq, adds completeness in bowing and prostration, recitation, humility, and attentiveness. The verb ***“establish”*** therefore suggests a practice maintained with its due form, rather than a movement performed carelessly. In its lexical discussion, the archive cites al-Aʿshāʾ using *ṣallā* for supplication, which helps explain why prayer is both service to God and a turning toward Him with need.

The phrase ***“donate from what We have provided for them”*** is similarly wider than a single transaction. Two reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās identify the obligatory alms: one through Ibn Isḥāq and Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad, from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and another through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah. A report attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk through Juwaybir describes voluntary support according to a person’s means before the detailed alms obligations, while the report through al-Suddī mentioned above includes provision for one’s household. Those are not identical legal claims, but they point toward giving from lawful provision rather than hoarding it as absolute personal possession. The verse places prayer and expenditure together: devotion to God is expressed both in worship and in care for others. Qur’an 2:4 will add continuity with earlier revelation, completing a portrait that holds trust, practice, and generosity together.

The verb translated ***“establish”*** also suggests maintaining something so it remains in place. In the source discussion, Arabic speakers could say that a market was established when buying and selling continued rather than stopped; by analogy, prayer is not merely begun but sustained with its required form. The metaphor therefore emphasizes continuity: as a market is kept functioning through buying and selling, prayer is maintained through regular performance rather than begun once and abandoned. This lexical analogy reinforces the verse’s joined picture of worship and generosity, which combines sustained devotion with sharing what God has provided.
verses.4:
> and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter

### **MEANING**

The description now reaches beyond the first community addressed. The mindful **believe in what was revealed to the Prophet** and in revelation sent before him, and they are certain of the Hereafter. The sequence makes continuity essential: acceptance of the Qur’an does not require rejecting earlier messengers, and respect for earlier revelation cannot be used to reject the message now being delivered. This is a faith that holds the messengers together and takes seriously the life beyond death.

### **ONE REVELATION, MANY MESSENGERS**

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted through Ibn Isḥāq and Muhammad ibn Abī Muhammad from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, says that these believers accept the Prophet’s message and what earlier messengers brought, ***“not distinguishing between them or denying what came from their Lord.”*** That wording clarifies the verse’s balance: the new revelation is not isolated from the earlier line, while the earlier line is not a reason to withhold belief from the present messenger.

Another transmitted explanation, carried by al-Suddī through a chain including Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ, identifies this description especially with People of Scripture who accepted the Qur’an. The preceding verses have already described belief in the unseen; this verse names belief in particular revelations and messengers. Some early readings therefore see two groups in the passage, while others understand all four verses as describing one kind of believer. In either case, the traits converge in a refusal to choose only the teachings that flatter one’s prior loyalties.

### **CERTAINTY ABOUT THE HEREAFTER**

The Hereafter is not a vague hope for a better future. In the report from Ibn ʿAbbās just mentioned, certainty includes resurrection, the Day of Judgement, Paradise and Hell, reckoning, and the balance of deeds. It is the world beyond this life in which people meet the consequence of what they have done. Qur’an 29:64 calls that final life the real life; this parallel underscores why the present verse says the believers have sure conviction rather than passing expectation.

The word *“certainty”* also matters for the contrast with the hypocrites described shortly afterward. A person who claims belief only to secure immediate safety behaves as though the visible present were all that counts. The believer described here acts with the unseen and the final return in view. That does not make earlier scriptures interchangeable in every detail; rather, it recognizes the common divine source affirmed in the transmitted explanation and accepts the revelation now addressed to the Prophet.

The verse therefore gathers the passage’s qualities into a coherent pattern: trust in what is unseen, commitment to prayer and generosity, fidelity to the line of revelation, and conviction about accountability. These descriptions prepare for the statement that follows: such people are **guided by their Lord** and attain success.

The name ***“Hereafter”*** itself signals that this life is followed by another abode. The source discussion explains the expression in relation to the earlier, present life and then lists the events that believers affirm there. The point is not to map every detail of that future in this verse, but to show why certainty about it changes present choices. A person who expects resurrection and reckoning has reason to preserve the unity of revelation and to act as though words and deeds will be brought to account.
verses.5:
> It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful

### **MEANING**

The verse gathers the two preceding descriptions under one conclusion. ***“It is they”*** points to the people just described: those who believe in the unseen and practice prayer and giving, and those who accept the revelation sent to the Prophet and before him. They stand on guidance from **their Lord**, and they are the ones who succeed. The emphasis is not merely that they have found a path, but that their direction comes from God and leads to a lasting outcome.

### **WHO IS INCLUDED?**

The early explanations differ over whether verses 2:3–4 describe one group or two. In a report transmitted through al-Suddī from Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ, the first description is associated with believers among the Arabs and the second with believing People of Scripture; the present verse then gathers both groups. Other explanations read the second description as an extension of the first, so that the same people carry all the qualities. The grammatical possibilities recorded in the archive reflect this interpretive question, but the basic point is shared: the praise follows the qualities already named.

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq explains ***“on guidance from their Lord”*** as ***“light from their Lord and uprightness in what came to them.”*** Guidance here is not self-congratulation or private certainty detached from revelation. It is a steadiness received from God and shown through belief, worship, generosity, and loyalty to His messengers. Qur’an 6:92 likewise calls revelation a blessed Book, reinforcing the relation between divine guidance and the life shaped by it.

### **WHAT SUCCESS MEANS**

The word translated ***“successful”*** carries the sense of attaining what one sought and escaping what one feared. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, also transmitted through Ibn Isḥāq, explains the successful as *“those who attain what they sought and are saved from the harm they fled.”* In this passage, that outcome is tied to faith and action, not status or ethnic identity. The two groups discussed in the reports are praised together because they share the qualities named in the verses.

The conclusion also answers the passage’s coming contrast. The disbelievers will be described as resistant to warning, while hypocrites will be shown trying to trade guidance for immediate advantage. The people of this verse do the opposite: they respond to what God reveals, let conviction shape their worship, and do not treat material provision as theirs alone. The language of guidance and success therefore describes both a path and its end.

Read with the preceding verses, the conclusion is neither an abstract promise nor a checklist detached from faith. It identifies a whole orientation: trust in God’s unseen promises, obedience in prayer, generosity with what He provides, and acceptance of revelation across the prophetic line. Those traits, rather than claims alone, explain why the Qur’an calls them guided and successful.

The demonstrative *“those”* gathers the descriptions rather than rewarding one group while excluding another. The report through al-Suddī explicitly has the two groups joined in the final praise; another explanation argues that people described by the same praiseworthy qualities should share the same praise. *“On guidance”* is therefore a stable footing, not a momentary feeling of certainty. The success promised here is the final attainment of what faith seeks, even when it is not identical with visible advantage in the present world.
verses.6:
> As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe

### **MEANING**

After describing believers, the passage turns to people who persist in rejecting the message. For them, warning or silence makes no difference: ***“they will never believe.”*** In context, this describes settled resistance, not a rule that every person who currently disbelieves is beyond reach. The verse names a group whose response has hardened; the following verse portrays that condition as a seal on perception. The warning remains meaningful even when this particular audience refuses it.

### **A SPECIFIC SETTING, A WIDER PATTERN**

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq, via Muhammad ibn Abī Muhammad from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, applies the words to Jewish scholars in and around Medina who rejected the Prophet despite recognizing signs of his mission. It says they rejected what had come to them while claiming attachment to earlier revelation. In that setting, *“disbelief”* means not simply lack of information, but covering or concealing what they knew. The same report situates the opening of the surah among named opponents, though the names themselves are not needed to understand the point.

Other explanations are preserved. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah connects the statement with God’s prior knowledge of who would believe, while al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas associates it with leaders who died in disbelief at Badr. These readings show how early interpreters connected the verse to historical opponents and divine foreknowledge. They do not require extending the description to every person who has not yet accepted the message.

### **THE LIMIT OF A WARNING**

The phrase ***“it is the same whether you warn them or not”*** describes the group’s response, not a failure in the warning itself. The Qur’an elsewhere condemns people who conceal revealed signs after they have been made clear; Qur’an 2:159 supplies a parallel to the Medina setting reported here. The burden falls on those who knowingly suppress or reject what has reached them, rather than on the messenger for having warned them.

The verse also prepares the contrast with the next portrait. These people are openly described as disbelievers, while the hypocrites will claim belief with their tongues and hide their opposition. Keeping the categories distinct matters: a hypocrite’s double speech is not the same as the public rejection named here, even though both refuse the guidance being offered.

The app’s wording ***“those who persist in disbelief”*** conveys the passage’s emphasis on persistence. A warning can be heard and weighed, but the people described have made rejection their settled response. The next verse’s image of a seal explains the spiritual consequence of that refusal; it should not be read as a reason to stop inviting, teaching, or hoping for others. The surah is diagnosing a particular posture and its outcome, not assigning the same destiny to all who begin outside belief.

The word translated ***“the same”*** expresses an equal result: warning and not warning make no difference to this group’s settled response. The archived language discussion compares it to ordinary speech in which two options are said to be equal for someone. This helps keep the sentence from sounding like a question about whether the Prophet should warn; it reports the effect of warning on the particular audience being described. Qur’an 2:159’s condemnation of hiding clear revelation supplies a nearby example of the knowing concealment associated with one reported setting.
verses.7:
> Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment

### **MEANING**

The image of a seal explains the closed response described in the previous verse. ***“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing”***; their eyes, too, are covered. These are images of blocked reception: counsel does not settle in the heart, warnings are not taken in, and signs are not properly seen. The verse presents this as a grave condition with a grave consequence, not as ordinary forgetfulness or a temporary difficulty in understanding.

### **HOW THE IMAGE WORKS**

The archive explains that a heart is like a container for knowledge and recognition, while hearing is a route by which news and warnings reach a person. Sealing a vessel closes access to what it holds; by analogy, a sealed heart no longer receives guidance in a responsive way. The wording distinguishes the senses: the heart and hearing are sealed, while ***“their sight is covered.”*** Qur’an 45:23 similarly speaks of a covering placed over a person’s perception, a parallel that supports the imagery without turning it into a physical medical diagnosis.

A report from Mujāhid, transmitted through al-Aʿmash, offers a gradual image: each sin closes part of the heart, until it is covered. Another report from him through Ibn Jurayj describes sins surrounding the heart until they meet and form a seal. These are explanatory images, not claims that the heart is literally a hand or vessel. They portray how repeated choices can narrow a person’s willingness to recognize what is true.

### **THE REPORT OF THE HEART’S STAIN**

A Prophetic report from Abū Hurayrah, transmitted by Abū Ṣāliḥ through al-Qaʿqāʿ and Ibn ʿAjlān, describes a dark mark appearing when a believer sins; repentance and seeking forgiveness polish the heart, while repeated sin allows the marks to accumulate. Its quoted explanation of the Qur’anic word *rān* is ***“the covering that gathers over their hearts.”*** Versions through Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān also appear in Aḥmad’s *Musnad*, Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, and Sunan Ibn Mājah. The report connects the image with Qur’an 83:14, where deeds are said to have left a stain over the heart.

This parallel helps hold accountability and hope together. The verse speaks of a seal upon those who persist in rejection, while the report describes repentance as a means of clearing a stain before it hardens. It would therefore be a mistake to treat every doubt, lapse, or struggle as proof that someone has been sealed. The surrounding passage addresses people who have chosen sustained denial despite warning and knowledge.

The final clause, ***“They will suffer a tremendous punishment,”*** makes clear that the image is also a warning. A person may still hear the words outwardly while refusing their meaning inwardly. The surah’s language asks the reader to take that danger seriously, without claiming access to the hidden state of any individual heart.

The separate clause about the eyes uses the image of a covering, not the same verb as the seal upon heart and hearing. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted through al-Suddī explains the distinction simply: they do not understand, hear, or see. This language describes the whole person’s refusal to receive guidance, while preserving the verse’s different images for different faculties. Its conclusion about punishment makes the outcome serious, but the comparison with repentance in the report about the heart’s stain shows that the surrounding Qur’anic imagery also distinguishes a warning from an irreversible diagnosis of every struggling person.
verses.8:
> And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers

### **MEANING**

The passage now turns from open denial to a more difficult contradiction: ***“We believe in Allah and the Last Day,”*** say people whose inward state does not match the profession. The problem is not that a sincere person has questions or struggles; it is that public profession is being used to conceal an opposite conviction. The next verses show the consequences of that split: attempted deception, growing inner sickness, and self-justification.

### **A DIVIDED PUBLIC AND PRIVATE LIFE**

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq locate the first audience among hypocrites in Medina, including people of the Aws and Khazraj and those aligned with them. Qatādah, transmitted by Maʿmar, identifies the passage through verse 16 as describing hypocrites; Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, similarly says the following verses portray them. These reports supply a historical setting, but the description is not a license to label whole tribes or later communities as hypocritical. It describes a chosen way of speaking and acting.

The sentence places profession beside denial: ***“We believe in Allah and the Last Day,”*** a claim contradicted by ***“they are not ˹true˺ believers.”*** In the explanation of Ibn Jurayj, the hypocrite’s outward statement conflicts with action, and the inner life conflicts with the public appearance. That contrast clarifies why the words alone are insufficient. The claim is not verified by saying it; its truth depends on what the speaker actually believes.

### **THE LAST DAY IS NOT A SLOGAN**

***“The Last Day”*** names the resurrection and final accounting, not simply another date or a vague symbol for moral seriousness. The previous descriptions of believers have emphasized conviction in the unseen and certainty about the Hereafter. Here, the same language is repeated by people whose inward state denies what their mouths affirm. Their claim therefore collapses precisely where the earlier portrait was coherent: they speak of accountability but live as if hidden motives and choices had no consequence.

Qur’an 2:9 immediately explains that their attempt to deceive reaches no further than themselves. That continuation is important: the verse is not presented as a detached definition of faith, but as the start of an account of self-damage. They may gain temporary safety by saying what others expect, yet the surah will portray that safety as no substitute for real faith.

The distinction also protects the reader from confusing sincere weakness with calculated duplicity. The verse condemns a mismatch deliberately maintained between public profession and inner denial. Its warning is about integrity: faith in God and **the Last Day** cannot be reduced to a phrase used only when it is advantageous.

The opening phrase ***“there are some”*** keeps the description specific: it identifies a portion of the people, not everyone who speaks about faith. The reports locating the first audience in Medina help explain the social pressure behind a double profession, but the moral pattern can be recognized wherever someone deliberately uses religious language as cover for a contrary allegiance. That application should follow the verse’s defined behavior, not a guess about another person’s hidden motives. The next verse’s focus on self-deception further shows that the passage is exposing a contradiction for correction, not inviting careless accusation.
verses.9:
> They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it

### **MEANING**

The hypocrites act as though they can mislead God and the believers by saying one thing publicly and holding another inwardly. The verse reverses that calculation: ***“they only deceive themselves,”*** even though **they fail to perceive it**. Their apparent success in managing other people’s impressions becomes a deeper loss, because they mistake temporary protection in this life for safety before God.

### **WHAT THEIR DECEPTION IS**

The archive describes their deception as presenting words of faith while concealing doubt and denial. Ibn Zayd, in a report carried by Ibn Wahb, identifies the group as hypocrites who show others that they believe. Ibn Jurayj explains the contradiction as *“his words against his actions, his hidden state against his public state.”* Their strategy is to keep the outward benefits of belonging while refusing the inward commitment that would make the profession true.

The phrase ***“deceive Allah”*** does not suggest that God is uninformed or can be tricked. It names the posture they adopt: they act as if a public statement could hide their real allegiance from the One who knows it. A similar formulation appears in Qur’an 4:142, which connects the hypocrites’ attempt to deceive with their performance of worship for public notice. The verse’s point is not that their ruse succeeds with God, but that they have mistaken a social appearance for a real escape.

### **WHY THEY DECEIVE THEMSELVES**

Their words can protect them from immediate consequences and win them a place among the believers in public life. The explanation in the archive makes that short-term benefit part of the irony: because they are treated outwardly according to what they profess, they suppose the same profession will carry them through the final judgement. Qur’an 57:13 gives a vivid parallel: hypocrites ask believers for light on the Day of Resurrection, only to find a barrier between them. That scene makes visible the false security the present verse describes.

The final words, ***“but they fail to perceive it,”*** explain why the deception continues. They do not recognize that their conduct is harming their own future; they mistake cunning for success. This blindness is not harmless ignorance, because the preceding verse already describes their conscious split between speech and conviction. Their failure lies in refusing to learn from the consequences of that choice.

The verse therefore turns the usual boast of the deceiver inside out. Others may be misled about what the hypocrite believes, but that does not change the reality known to God. By pursuing immediate protection while sacrificing truth, they become the primary victims of their own strategy. The following image of sickness develops the same idea: an inner condition grows worse while its bearer fails to recognize what is happening.

The archive recognizes the obvious short-term effect: by their profession, these people may be treated in worldly dealings as members of the believing community. Yet that apparent gain is not the same as deceiving believers in the ultimate sense, since it cannot make the hidden denial true or erase accountability. Ibn Zayd’s report through Ibn Wahb describes the public appearance they adopt; Qur’an 57:13 shows the eventual separation between them and believers. The verse thus answers the question implicit in their strategy: a mask can alter how people respond now, but it cannot rescue the wearer from the result of the choice.
verses.10:
> There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies

### **MEANING**

The sickness is in the hypocrites’ hearts, and it increases as they persist in doubt and false profession. The image describes a diseased inner conviction, not a bodily illness. God’s letting it increase is presented alongside their own lies: they continue to answer revelation with suspicion and concealment, so the next disclosure deepens rather than cures the disorder they have chosen. The **painful punishment** names the eventual consequence of maintaining that course.

### **WHAT THE SICKNESS IS**

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq, and to Qatādah through Ibn al-Mubārak, explain the sickness as doubt and uncertainty in matters of faith. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas describes it as doubt about God’s affair; Ibn Zayd clarifies that the illness is in religion, not the body. The archive’s image of someone who *“makes an illness”* of a decision helps convey wavering: the hypocrites neither settle into sincere conviction nor openly accept responsibility for rejection.

The phrase ***“There is sickness in their hearts”*** therefore speaks about their inward stance toward the Prophet and the message. Their lips profess belief, but uncertainty and denial remain active beneath the surface. The passage does not use sickness to mock people who are physically ill or to stigmatize ordinary mental distress. It is a moral and spiritual metaphor tied specifically to the double life described in verses 8–9.

### **HOW IT INCREASES**

The archived explanation relates the increase to new commands and revelations. When further duties arrive, believers can add trust to trust by accepting them; those who already resist can add suspicion to suspicion. Qur’an 9:124–125 makes the same contrast: a newly revealed surah increases faith for believers, while people with **sickness in their hearts** gain further impurity. This parallel helps explain the wording without making God the author of an arbitrary illness: the same message is received differently according to the hearer’s chosen response.

The final phrase follows the app’s reading ***“for their lies.”*** The archive records two recitations: one meaning that the hypocrites lie in claiming belief, and another that they reject the truth. It argues from the surrounding account that the false profession has already been stated, so lying is a direct fit; a related Qur’anic passage, Qur’an 63:1–2, likewise calls the hypocrites liars when they assert belief with their tongues while concealing denial.

The two readings illuminate connected aspects of the same conduct, but the app’s translation preserves the first. The **painful punishment** is not attached to a passing uncertainty; it is linked to a knowingly false claim and a sustained refusal to correct it. In this way the image of sickness carries the argument forward: what begins as concealed doubt is strengthened by each act of deception.

The adjective translated ***“painful”*** is explained in the archive as an active description: an affliction that causes pain. Reports attributed to al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar and to al-Ḍaḥḥāk through Juwaybir preserve that concise gloss. The word prevents the metaphor of sickness from becoming abstract: the inner disorder has a real consequence. At the same time, the explanation of increasing doubt remains tied to the passage’s sequence of revelation and response, rather than to the idea that every fresh question is blameworthy. The warning concerns the lie maintained after the truth has been recognized.
verses.11:
> When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”

### **MEANING**

The warning is about a life that damages the moral order: ***“Do not spread corruption in the land.”*** The people addressed answer that they are only making things right. The contradiction is the verse’s point. They sincerely present themselves as reformers, yet their allegiance to denial and their actions undermine the very trust and obedience that make a community sound. The next verse states the judgment plainly: their self-description does not determine what their conduct is.

### **WHAT CORRUPTION MEANS HERE**

The archive preserves a range of explanatory emphasis. A report through al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ with explanations attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, glosses corruption as disbelief and sinful action. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, transmitted through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar and his father, explains the warning as ***“do not disobey in the land”*** and says that disobedience disorders what obedience sets right. This meaning is wider than physical destruction: deliberate falsehood, breach of trust, and assistance to hostility can also corrupt relations between people.

The historical explanation in the surrounding passage concerns hypocrites in Medina who claimed to be helping reconcile believers and People of Scripture. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq gives that as their stated reason for calling themselves reformers; Mujāhid, through Ibn Jurayj, says they defended their conduct as guidance. Their claim may have sounded plausible to them, but the passage measures it against what they concealed and supported, not the label they chose for themselves.

### **REFORMER OR CORRUPTOR?**

The app’s phrase ***“We are only peace-makers!”*** captures that self-understanding. The issue is not that peace-making is wrong; the verse condemns a claim to peace that accompanies disobedience, double-dealing, and support for those opposing the message. The distinction is essential: good intentions asserted by an actor cannot by themselves make harmful conduct beneficial. A person may persuade themselves that compromise is reform while the result is further distrust and injustice.

The passage also expands beyond its first audience. Though early interpreters connect it to Medinan hypocrites, the pattern applies to anyone whose deeds fit the described conduct. Qur’an 2:30 soon repeats the language of corruption and bloodshed in the angels’ question about human life, showing why the concern is larger than a private mistake. Here, however, the emphasis is on the hypocrisy of claiming to repair society while sustaining a course that weakens its relationship with God and with other people.

The verse therefore refuses to let self-presentation settle the matter. Its warning exposes the difference between stated aims and actual effects, preparing the direct correction in the next line.

The word translated *“corruption”* is not limited here to one public offense. The accompanying explanations include disobedience, disbelief, concealing one’s real position, and backing those who oppose the believers. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq gives the hypocrites’ own account of reform as an attempt to reconcile the two sides; the response is that reconciliation cannot be built on a hidden alliance that sustains hostility. The verse asks the reader to judge the whole pattern, not the attractive name attached to it.
verses.12:
> Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it

### **MEANING**

This short verse answers the hypocrites’ claim in the previous one. They say they are making things right; the Qur’an replies that ***“they are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.”*** The emphatic opening leaves no ambiguity about which account is accepted. Their lack of awareness is part of the diagnosis: they have come to mistake their own disobedience for sound judgment, and so the harm they cause confirms neither their intentions nor their self-image.

### **THE PASSAGE CORRECTS THEIR SELF-IMAGE**

The force of the statement depends on its position. Qur’an 2:11 first gives the exchange: people are told not to spread corruption, then answer that they are reformers. Verse 12 supplies the judgment they refuse to make about themselves. The commentary in the archive explains the corruption as opposition to God’s command, neglect of obligations, and the destructive consequences of false profession. It contrasts those actions with the believers who call them away from wrongdoing.

The line is not a separate maxim claiming that everyone who disagrees with a religious authority is corrupt. Its reference is anchored to the group just described and the pattern of conduct attributed to them. The immediate context identifies the problem as deliberate concealment and support for hostility while claiming an opposite purpose. To apply the warning responsibly, one must attend to that full pattern rather than seize on the word *“corruptors”* as an insult for opponents.

### **BLINDNESS TO CONSEQUENCES**

The phrase ***“they fail to perceive it”*** is more than lack of information. Their answer in verse 11 shows that they have a story about what they are doing; the failure is that they cannot recognize how their actions contradict the good they claim to seek. This echoes the end of verse 9, where they do not perceive that their deception harms themselves. In both cases, the short-term account they give of their actions obscures their deeper consequences.

The passage’s language of awareness is therefore morally significant. They are not portrayed as people who have never heard a correction: the preceding verse begins, *“When they are told.”* Yet correction meets self-certainty rather than reflection. Instead of asking whether their conduct should change, they insist they are already the reformers. The repeated contrast between perception and blindness prepares the next verse, where they label sincere believers as foolish and are told that the judgment actually applies to them.

Read together, the two verses make a compact argument. A person’s claim to be doing good is not enough; the conduct and allegiance behind it must be examined. The Qur’an names the contradiction even when those caught in it cannot see it, and invites the reader to learn from the correction rather than repeat it.

The word *“indeed”* marks the sentence as a correction to the claim just reported, while *“they”* identifies the same speakers rather than introducing a new group. The repeated root for corruption also binds the verses together: first comes their denial of wrongdoing, then the Qur’an’s clear naming of it. Their blindness is shown in the gap between being told to stop and insisting that they already know best. That gap, rather than a mere difference in vocabulary, is why the denial itself becomes part of the portrait.
verses.13:
> And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know

### **MEANING**

The hypocrites are urged to believe as the sincere community believes. They answer with contempt, calling those believers foolish; the verse reverses the insult. ***“It is they who are fools”*** because they sacrifice sound judgment for a double life, yet ***“they do not know.”*** The passage is not praising people for being naïve. It presents sincere faith as a reasoned response, and exposes the folly of rejecting it while mistaking calculation for wisdom.

### **WHO ARE THE PEOPLE?**

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk explains the command as: accept Muhammad as a prophet and messenger, affirm that what has been sent to him is true, and believe in the Hereafter as his Companions do. The definite expression translated ***“as others believe”*** therefore points to people known in the setting of the verse—the believers around the Prophet—not to an unspecified majority whose numbers alone make them right. Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and other Companions through al-Suddī, as well as al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, identify the ***“fools”*** in the hypocrites’ taunt as the Companions of Muhammad.

The answer exposes an inversion: the people whose belief leads them to prayer, generosity, and confidence in revelation are called irrational, while those protecting a divided allegiance present themselves as discerning. The charge says more about the speakers’ standards than about the believers’ intelligence. Qur’an 4:5 uses the same Arabic word for people whose judgment is not ready to manage wealth responsibly; the shared idea is poor discernment, though the contexts are different.

### **WHAT TRUE FOOLISHNESS COSTS**

The verse’s reply is not merely that the hypocrites have chosen the wrong social side. The surrounding descriptions show what their choice does: they conceal disbelief, attempt to deceive, and call corruption reform. A report from Ibn Jurayj, as cited in the preceding account, describes their hidden and public states as contradicting each other. The foolishness lies in harming their own final interests while imagining that the arrangement protects them.

The phrase ***“but they do not know”*** parallels ***“but they fail to perceive it”*** in verse 12. In both places the problem is a damaged ability to evaluate one’s own conduct. The hypocrites call believers fools because those believers refuse to join their strategy; the Qur’an evaluates wisdom by whether a choice leads to truth and lasting success, not by whether it avoids immediate social risk.

The verse also helps distinguish sincere weakness from hypocrisy. A believer can lack knowledge or make a mistake without using the word *“faith”* to conceal a settled rejection. Here the criticism is directed at the intentional contempt and self-deception of the people already described. The call is simple—believe as the believers believe—but its simplicity exposes a deep refusal to treat revelation as a serious claim.

The Arabic *safīh* in the archived explanation means someone weak in judgment and unable to recognize where benefit and harm lie; it is not simply a synonym for poor or socially powerless. The hypocrites use the term to dismiss the Companions, but the passage evaluates judgment by its destination. The believers accept the message and prepare for accountability, whereas their critics protect a divided allegiance and call that caution. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk makes the call concrete: acknowledge the Prophet and the truth of what has been sent to him.
verses.14:
> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”

### **MEANING**

The verse depicts two audiences and two incompatible professions. In front of believers, the hypocrites say they believe; in private with ***“their evil associates”***; there, they reaffirm their allegiance to rejection and dismiss their public profession as a joke. The scene makes the split visible through changing company: they present whichever identity protects them in the moment. Their private statement exposes the public one as a tactic rather than a sincere change of heart.

### **WHO ARE THEIR ASSOCIATES?**

The Arabic word *shayāṭīn* can mean devils, but the reports here explain it as human leaders and companions who persist in evil. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī calls them the leading figures among the disbelievers; Qatādah, transmitted through Saʿīd, describes them as *“their leaders in evil.”* Other explanations associated with Mujāhid include companions among hypocrites and polytheists. This range supports the app’s contextual rendering ***“evil associates”*** without requiring the phrase to mean supernatural beings in this scene.

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk describe Jewish men telling the Prophet’s companions that they shared their religion, then returning to their own group. Another report, through Ibn Isḥāq from Muhammad ibn Abī Muhammad via ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, speaks of leaders who urged denial of the message. These are reports about a specific Medinan setting; they should not be converted into accusations against every later member of a religious community.

### **THE ADMISSION OF MOCKERY**

The final words are direct: ***“we were only mocking.”*** The early explanations agree that the phrase means making fun of the believers, not merely keeping a harmless joke between friends. The hypocrites treat their public profession as a performance and their private rejection as the truth. Their speech changes, but the verse indicates that the inner allegiance does not.

The wording also connects this scene back to the earlier claim, ***“We believe in Allah and the Last Day.”*** The two statements cannot both be sincere when the speakers explicitly tell their associates that the first was a pretense. The public words may secure safety or access, but they do not create faith. This is why the passage’s focus is on the contradiction itself, not on whether the believers were foolish to trust a statement they heard.

The movement between groups previews the next verse’s answer. The hypocrites think their mockery is a successful way to manage others; the Qur’an replies that the consequence will return upon them. Their private confidence is therefore not proof of control, but another part of the self-deception already named in verses 9 and 12.

The verb describing their private gathering is also discussed in the archive. Early grammarians explain *“turning to”* their associates as movement away from the believers toward a chosen audience, which sharpens the scene’s social contrast. They are not merely speaking differently by accident; they choose which community to reassure and which one to please. The report from Qatādah through Saʿīd identifies the private audience as the leaders of wrongdoing, while other reports include companions among unbelievers. This explains the translation without requiring a literal supernatural reading of the word for devils.
verses.15:
> Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance

### **MEANING**

The app renders the response as ***“Allah will throw their mockery back at them.”*** The verse answers the hypocrites’ boast by declaring that their apparent advantage will not last. It then says that they are left to continue in defiance, wandering without clear direction. The language turns their own posture against them: they mock the believers and imagine they are in control, while their choices deepen the confusion and punishment awaiting them.

### **WHAT DIVINE MOCKERY MEANS**

Early explanations describe this phrase in several related ways. Some connect it to the hypocrites’ eventual exposure and humiliation, as in Qur’an 57:13, where they ask the believers for light and are separated from them. Others describe it as requital: the hypocrites’ mockery is answered with a just consequence, not with a matching act of wrongdoing. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk glosses it as *“He ridicules them as a requital against them.”* The wording thus announces judgment in terms that fit their own behavior.

A further explanation in the archive considers how mockery works in ordinary speech: someone may appear to say or do what pleases another while the actual result humiliates or harms that person. Applied here, the hypocrites are allowed the outward appearance they prize for a time, then their inward denial is exposed. Qur’an 3:178 similarly warns that a temporary delay is not necessarily a benefit; it can leave wrongdoing to accumulate before its consequence arrives. These parallels clarify the image without implying that divine justice is a human prank.

### **LEFT TO WANDER**

The word rendered ***“leaving them to continue”*** is explained in reports in two complementary ways. A report through al-Suddī, with explanations attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and others, glosses it as granting respite; Mujāhid, transmitted through Ibn al-Mubārak from Ibn Jurayj, explains it as increasing. The surrounding phrase combines delay and deepening: they are permitted to persist, and their chosen defiance grows more entrenched.

Their ***“wandering blindly in their defiance”*** captures *yaʿmahūn*, explained by Qatādah through Saʿīd and Mujāhid through Ibn Abī Najīḥ as straying or moving about uncertainly. It is not innocent lack of a map. The preceding verses show repeated opportunities to turn back, met with self-justification and contempt. In Qur’an 6:110, the same pattern is described as being left to wander in transgression after earlier refusal.

The verse’s two halves therefore belong together. **Their mockery** returns as judgment, and the delay they mistake for safety becomes part of their loss. The passage describes the outcome of persistent defiance, not a license for believers to retaliate or mock in turn.

The phrase ***“wandering blindly in their defiance”*** combines two ideas: exceeding a limit and losing one’s way within that excess. Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk gloss the state as moving uncertainly in disbelief; Mujāhid’s explanation through Ibn Abī Najīḥ likewise emphasizes hesitation and confusion. The verse does not describe the hypocrites as calmly advancing toward a known good. It depicts a course that grows more extreme while the people on it become less able to see where it leads.
verses.16:
> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided

### **MEANING**

The hypocrites are portrayed as traders who exchange ***“guidance for misguidance”***, only to discover that the deal produces no profit. The metaphor explains the cost of their choice: they give up a path that could lead to truth and lasting success for the short-lived advantages of concealment. ***“This trade is profitless”*** is not just a figure of speech about poor tactics; it measures the choice against what the Hereafter will bring.

### **WHAT WAS EXCHANGED?**

Early reports express the metaphor in several ways. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq glosses the exchange as disbelief for faith. Another report, through al-Suddī from Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ, says they took error and left guidance. Qatādah, transmitted through Saʿīd, describes them as preferring misguidance to guidance. Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says they believed and then disbelieved. These explanations differ over whether an earlier real faith is implied.

The surrounding passage, however, has already said that their profession was not true belief. That context allows the commercial image to work without claiming that they once held sincere faith: they abandon the guidance available to them and take up error in its place. The exchange can be a choice between options, not only a conversion from a state once possessed. Qur’an 41:17 uses similar language for people who preferred blindness to guidance.

### **WHY THE TRADE FAILS**

A merchant profits by receiving something more valuable than what was surrendered. Here the exchange runs in the opposite direction. The hypocrites may gain a measure of social safety or material ease, but they lose truthful direction and expose themselves to the punishment described earlier. The source preserves Qatādah’s vivid contrast: they left ***“guidance for misguidance,”*** community for division, and security for fear. These are the costs of their choice even before the final accounting.

The line ***“they are not ˹rightly˺ guided”*** completes the image. A successful trade would bring the buyer toward a good destination; this transaction leaves them farther from it. Their inability to recognize the loss repeats the blindness named in the surrounding verses. They think their concealment has protected them, but the passage judges outcomes by more than immediate advantage.

The language of buying and selling is especially apt after their claims to reform and their private admission of mockery. Each verse strips away another self-description: their claims to peacemaking, wisdom, and profitable trade all fail. The repeated image of loss prepares for the parables that follow, where a brief flash of light cannot provide lasting direction.

The commercial image makes the loss measurable. A trader gains only if the thing received is worth more than what was surrendered; here the hypocrites trade away a truthful path for temporary protection and confusion. The archive reports Qatādah’s contrast between guidance and misguidance, community and division, safety and fear. These are not unrelated slogans: each names a benefit they imagine they have secured and the deeper opposite that their choice produces. The closing judgment that they lack guidance completes the metaphor by showing that the transaction has moved them away from their destination.
verses.17:
> Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see

### **MEANING**

The first parable gives a picture of borrowed visibility. Someone lights a fire; it illuminates the surroundings, then the light is taken away and darkness remains. The comparison is not primarily about the person’s body but about the temporary benefit the hypocrites obtain from outwardly professing faith. For a time, that profession lets them move among believers and receive the protections of community; it does not give them the inward light that would guide them when the outward advantage ends.

### **THE FIRE AND ITS BRIEF LIGHT**

Reports attributed to Qatādah, including one transmitted through Maʿmar, identify the fire’s light with the profession of divine unity. He explains that the words allowed the hypocrite to eat, drink, marry, and remain safe in worldly life. The fire therefore illuminates what is nearby, just as public profession secures immediate social benefits. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq describes people who recognize the truth and speak of it, then extinguish that light through denial. These accounts emphasize different sides of the image: practical benefit and moral recognition.

The archive also preserves an explanation through al-Suddī, in a chain that includes Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, comparing the hypocrite to someone who enters a dark place, lights a fire, sees what to avoid, and then loses the light. The image is an analogy, not a claim that every person described once possessed sincere and complete faith. The surrounding verses have already distinguished their public words from their concealed conviction.

### **DARKNESS AND EXPOSURE**

When the fire’s light disappears, the person cannot see a safe route. The app’s ***“leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see”*** expresses that loss of direction. Qur’an 57:13 provides a parallel scene in which hypocrites ask believers to share **their light** at the final gathering and are separated by a barrier. That passage makes the parable’s warning concrete: a public label of faith cannot supply light at the moment when inward truth is revealed.

The shift from brightness to darkness also explains why the parable follows the account of self-deception and a failed trade. What they treated as illumination was temporary; when it ends, there is nothing stable underneath. The short light makes the resulting darkness more striking, since the person has briefly seen enough to know what is missing.

The verse thus portrays not a random loss but the consequence of relying on appearance. The hypocrites use a profession that gives them outward standing while withholding the trust that could guide them. When the borrowed benefit ends, they are left **unable to see**. The next verse names that incapacity through the image of deafness, muteness, and blindness.

The worldly privileges named in the reports include not only immediate safety but also being treated as part of the Muslim community in marriage, inheritance, and shared public life. The fire’s light therefore helps explain why the outward profession could seem useful even to someone who did not believe inwardly. Another report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah links the extinguished light with losing that worldly standing at death. The details vary, but each explanation distinguishes a temporary social benefit from the lasting illumination of sincere faith.
verses.18:
> They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺

### **MEANING**

The verse describes the hypocrites as ***“deaf, dumb, and blind”*** to guidance, then says they do not ***“return to the right path”***. The language is figurative, not a claim about physical disability. They fail to hear what could correct them, do not speak the truth they recognize, and do not see the evidence that would lead them back. The three images gather the perceptual failures already suggested by the fire parable into one compact judgment.

### **DEAF, MUTE, BLIND TO WHAT?**

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq gloss the phrase as being deaf to good; another explanation from him, transmitted through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says they do not hear or see guidance or understand it. Qatādah, through Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, distinguishes the faculties: deaf to truth and unwilling to hear it, blind to truth and unwilling to see it, and unable to speak it. The point is not a lack of sensory ability but a settled refusal to receive and affirm the message.

The order matters. Their lack of hearing and sight is connected to their purchase of error, not to an inability imposed on innocent people. The previous verse showed how outward profession can give temporary light without stable insight; this verse explains the inner inability to turn that flash into a lasting change. Qur’an 2:7 used the related image of a seal on the heart and hearing, reinforcing the passage’s language of blocked reception.

### **NO RETURN TO THE PATH**

A report from Qatādah explains ***“they will never return”*** as not repenting or taking heed. Another explanation, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī, says they do not return to Islam. These are related descriptions of a continuing refusal. The verse does not make a general statement that no sinner can repent; it describes the group whose defining feature in this passage is persistence in concealment and rejection.

The contrast between return and wandering also links the parables. The person without light cannot find a way back, and the people with no hearing, speech, or sight do not respond to direction. Yet the narrative still functions as a warning for readers: the Qur’an names the end of stubborn refusal in order to make the danger visible before it is reached.

A refusal to hear truth can become habitual; so can speaking against it and looking away from its signs. The verse’s compressed language gathers those habits into a portrait of spiritual incapacity. It follows the failed trade in verse 16 and the extinguished light in verse 17, showing why temporary public benefit cannot substitute for repentance and real guidance.

The source also notes that *“return”* can be expressed as turning back from error or repenting. Qatādah’s transmitted gloss says they do not repent or take heed; a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī says they do not return to Islam. Both fit the image of someone who has repeatedly ignored direction until the route back is no longer sought. The language is severe because the surrounding portrait is severe, but its purpose remains admonition: the reader is shown what persistent refusal leads to before imitating it.
verses.19:
> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺

### **MEANING**

A second parable places the hypocrites inside a rain-filled storm. Night, crashing thunder, and sudden flashes create a scene of fear and disorientation. The image conveys a fearful and unstable response to revelation: they hear warnings that unsettle them, but try to shut them out rather than face what they mean. The final statement, ***“Allah encompasses the disbelievers,”*** assures that their fear and evasions do not put them beyond God’s power.

### **THE STORM AS A PARABLE**

The early explanations generally understand *ṣayyib* as rain, though Mujāhid is also reported as describing it as spring rain. The archive records different explanations of thunder in the natural scene—some authorities call it an angel driving the clouds, while others describe wind—but the parable’s central force lies in the storm’s sensory pressure and the travelers’ fear. Night hides the road, and abrupt flashes disclose it only for an instant; the storm’s force leaves those outside unsure where to go.

A report attributed to al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar compares the scene to travelers on a road in a dark, rainy night. They move forward when lightning shows the road and become confused when it fades. Qatādah, transmitted through Maʿmar, applies the shifting conditions to hypocrites who are comfortable when Islam appears to bring ease but falter when hardship arrives. Qur’an 22:11 offers a close parallel in its description of someone who worships at the edge, reassured by good fortune but turning away when tested.

### **FEAR AND EVASION**

The fingers in the ears make the response physical: they fear the warning but do not want to hear it. Some reports describe people at the Prophet’s gatherings fearing that a verse might expose them; the archive itself notes uncertainty about the chain of that particular account. Its more general explanation is that the Qur’anic threats are like thunder to people who suspect the warning may be true but still doubt it. The fear does not become faith merely because it is intense.

The clause ***“for fear of death”*** carries the image of someone trying to escape the storm’s danger. The hypocrites’ outward words similarly aim to protect their lives and possessions, while their inward state remains divided. They may briefly find the message compelling or beneficial, yet dread its consequences and avoid hearing what it demands.

### **NO ESCAPE FROM ACCOUNTABILITY**

Reports attributed to Mujāhid through Ibn Abī Najīḥ explain ***“encompasses the disbelievers”*** as gathering them, and by a report from Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq as bringing the threatened punishment upon them. Both readings deny that hiding, fear, or temporary conformity can place someone outside divine knowledge and judgment. The storm parable therefore describes not merely distress, but a response that leaves the hearer exposed because he will not accept the guidance offered.

The archive’s natural explanations of thunder are not identical, and they need not be settled in order to understand the parable. What matters in the image is that the storm’s sound and flashes frighten the travelers while giving them only unstable visibility. Reports attributed to Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ map this to people who fear the Qur’an’s warnings and yet move forward when they see a worldly advantage. This gesture corresponds to an attempt to block the warning, not to a lack of sound. The phrase ***“Allah encompasses the disbelievers”*** closes off the fantasy that evasion can make the threat disappear.
verses.20:
> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

### **MEANING**

The lightning flashes so intensely that it seems ready to ***“snatch away”*** the travelers’ sight. They move while light lasts and halt once darkness returns. The parable completes the account of the storm by showing how conditional the hypocrites’ progress is. They advance when faith seems to promise something they want, but lose direction when hardship or uncertainty interrupts that benefit. The closing warning adds that the very faculties they use to navigate are within God’s power to remove.

### **MOVING ONLY IN THE FLASHES**

Reports in the archive connect the lightning with the outward profession of faith. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, transmitted through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar, compares the travelers’ movement to a hypocrite who speaks a word of faith and briefly sees a way forward, then falls back into confusion when doubt returns. Qatādah, through Maʿmar, describes the moments of light as worldly advantages—wealth, livestock, safety, and success—that reassure the hypocrite that his present course is working. Qur’an 22:11 again offers a parallel: a person’s commitment shifts with the balance between benefit and trial.

The phrase ***“Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light”*** does not describe steady conviction. It shows movement borrowed from an external flash. They can take a few steps, but cannot sustain a direction when the light disappears. In contrast, the believers described at the start of the surah act from conviction in realities they cannot see; the hypocrites here move only when the immediate circumstances appear favorable.

### **HEARING, SIGHT, AND POWER**

The final threat returns to the senses named in the storm scene. They put fingers in their ears and are dazzled by lightning, yet ***“He could have taken away their hearing and sight”*** if He willed. The source explains that these two faculties are singled out because they have just appeared in the parable, not because other parts of human life are outside divine power. The warning is linked to the preceding statement that God encompasses the disbelievers: neither their evasion nor their temporary movement can defeat His authority.

The app’s wording ***“Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight”*** is a conditional warning, not a report that He has already removed their physical senses. The end of the verse, ***“Allah is Most Capable of everything,”*** gives the reason they should take that warning seriously. The same God who grants perception can withhold it, and no created power can prevent His judgement.

The rainstorm parable thus distinguishes brief reaction from stable guidance. Fear can make someone cover his ears; temporary brightness can make him take a step. Neither amounts to a settled return. The passage invites the hearer to continue beyond the flash and accept the message before the opportunity to respond is gone.

The verb behind ***“snatch away”*** carries the sense of seizing something suddenly, which intensifies the flash: the light is not a calm, lasting sunrise but a startling brightness that nearly overwhelms the eye. A report through al-Rabīʿ describes the travelers’ changing movement; Qatādah’s report through Maʿmar emphasizes the hypocrites’ calculations about wealth, safety, and hardship. Together they explain why the alternation matters: their progress depends on conditions, not settled conviction. The verse’s warning about human perception then reminds them that these capacities are gifts, not possessions they can secure against God’s will.
verses.21:
> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺

### **MEANING**

The address widens to all people after the surah has described believers, open rejecters, and hypocrites. The call is to worship the Creator of the present audience and earlier generations, with the aim of becoming ***“mindful of Him”***. Worship here is not only ritual: the early explanation includes obedience and exclusive devotion. The reason offered is creation itself. The One who gave life has the strongest claim to gratitude and service; created beings cannot rival their Creator.

### **WORSHIP AND ONENESS**

A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Isḥāq glosses ***“worship your Lord”*** as *“make your Lord one”*. The broader language explanation in the archive defines worship as humble obedience and submission. These meanings belong together: to worship God alone is to direct ultimate devotion and obedience to Him, not simply to affirm that He exists while assigning His place to other powers. The verse’s reason is explicit—He created the audience and earlier generations.

The scope is universal. The address is not limited to the believers just praised or to one historical community; it reaches the groups whose responses have been described and people beyond them. The creator’s claim is therefore made before the audience is divided by its response. Qur’an 10:31 supplies a close parallel by asking who provides, governs, and brings life from death; the answer is God, even among people who still associate others with Him.

### **THE PURPOSE OF MINDFULNESS**

The phrase ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺”*** expresses the aim of worship. Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, is reported to gloss it as *“so that you obey”*. The explanation does not make the outcome a matter of uncertainty in God’s knowledge. It describes the purpose for which people are commanded: obedience and exclusive worship can guard them from divine displeasure and shape them into the mindful community described earlier.

The passage thus moves from description to invitation. The prior verses showed what faithfulness and refusal look like; now the hearer is addressed directly and asked to respond. The call does not leave worship as an abstract idea, because the next verse will name signs of provision in the world people inhabit. Creation is both a gift sustaining life and a reason to recognize who alone deserves worship.

The verse’s reasoning is deliberately accessible: the One ***“who created you and those before you”*** is not one rival among many. Gratitude and obedience should follow from recognizing the source of life. In this way the universal address connects the earlier portraits to the practical command that follows.

The address follows the earlier portraits deliberately. Neither the open disbeliever nor the hypocrite is excluded from hearing the command; the call comes after their responses have been described. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī says the verse addresses both groups, while the wider wording reaches all accountable people. The invitation is therefore not a reward reserved for those already described as faithful. It offers a way to turn from the earlier failures by recognizing the Creator and directing worship to Him.
verses.22:
> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺

The verse names ordinary signs of provision: the earth is made a settled place for human life, with ***“the sky”*** pictured as a protective ***“canopy”***; rain descends, and fruit grows as food. These gifts support the command that came before: worship the Lord who created you. The concluding prohibition follows from the same reasoning. Since the Creator and provider is one, people should not assign equals to Him in worship or obedience while depending on what He alone provides.

### **A WORLD MADE LIVABLE**

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and other early authorities through al-Suddī describe the earth as a place to walk, settle, and dwell; Qatādah, through Saʿīd, glosses it as a resting-place or expanse. The image translated ***“a place of settlement for you”*** is not a technical map of the earth’s shape. It points to its accessibility and usefulness as a home. The sky is described as a canopy or roof; a report through al-Suddī and another from Qatādah use that sheltering comparison.

Rain links the sky to food. The archive explains that water descends and enables plants and fruit to grow, making provision for human beings. The point is not simply that people observe natural processes, but that their lives depend on a chain of gifts they did not create. Qur’an 10:31 makes the same argument by asking who sends provision from heaven and earth; the verse says that even those who associate partners recognize that God is the provider.

The word *nidd* means an equal, counterpart, or match. Early explanations include idols and other supposed deities; one report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī also warns against treating people as equals whose commands are obeyed in disobedience to God. This does not erase the app’s phrase ***“set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺”***; it clarifies that worship includes more than a ritual act. The question is whether a created being is given the ultimate loyalty that belongs to the Creator.

The early explanations differ over whether the immediate audience is all polytheists and People of Scripture or specifically People of Scripture. The wider address to humanity, and the Qur’anic acknowledgement that Arab polytheists recognized God as creator, support reading the warning as relevant to anyone who knows the source of provision but gives another an equal place.

The verse therefore joins gratitude to worship. The earth, sky, rain, and fruit are not rivals to God but signs of dependence on Him. Their ordinary familiarity should make the command more intelligible, not less urgent.

The phrase ***“do not set up equals”*** reaches beyond images made of stone. The explanation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Suddī includes people obeyed when they call for disobedience to God, while another report identifies the equals as deities given the place of God. The shared issue is misplaced ultimate allegiance. Qur’an 10:31 makes the tension explicit: people can acknowledge that God creates and provides while still assigning worship or obedience to others. verses.23:
> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true

### **MEANING**

The challenge addresses anyone who doubts that the revelation came from God: produce a single surah like it, and summon the helpers on whom you rely. The question is not whether people can write or speak; it is whether those who call the Qur’an a human invention can meet its challenge in the language they know.
